set.text: Before the final of the city chess championship, Viktor Sorokin was cocksure. He told reporters he would beat “the schoolgirl” in under thirty moves. His opponent, fifteen-year-old Zainab Musa, said nothing. During the game Viktor tried every kind of gamesmanship allowed by the rules: he spent ages over the simplest moves and took long walks around the hall, all to make her wait and lose focus. Zainab remained imperturbable. She sat with an unblinking gaze fixed on the board, as if he were not even there. On move twenty-two, she offered her queen. It looked like a blunder, and Viktor grabbed it at once. Six moves later, his king was trapped. She had managed to outmaneuver him completely, and he left the hall ignominiously, ignoring the reporters he had spoken to so proudly the day before.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “gamesmanship” mean?
options: playing many games at the same time
a love of competition
cheating by moving pieces illegally
great skill at planning moves
fair and generous behavior toward an opponent
using tactics that are allowed but questionable to gain an advantage
qs.why: Stalling over easy moves and wandering the hall were within the rules but meant to unsettle her. They were not illegal moves.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “cocksure” mean?
options: angry and impatient
polite and modest
tired and bored
certain because of careful study of the facts
nervous and worried
far too sure of himself, in a proud and annoying way
qs.why: He boasted he would win in under thirty moves and lost. His confidence was arrogant, not based on facts.

qs.q: Why did Viktor take Zainab's queen?
options: The rules forced him to take it
He wanted to make her wait longer
It won him the game
Zainab asked him to take it
It looked like a mistake, but it was a trap that led to his defeat
He was running out of time
qs.why: The queen offer “looked like a blunder,” and six moves later his king was trapped. Taking it lost him the game.

why: Factual error: tapping a pen and sighing loudly at the board are not 'allowed by the rules' in rated chess (FIDE Laws Art. 11.5 forbids distracting or annoying the opponent in any manner). Replaced with genuinely legal gamesmanship (stalling on own clock, walking in the hall) and updated the gamesmanship 'why'.

set.text: Our group of twelve set out at seven, and by noon I was clearly the tenderfoot. The others had hiked these mountains for years; I had bought my boots the week before. We had to traipse for hours across rocky slopes, and my legs ached with every step. Then came the ridge: a narrow path with vertiginous drops on both sides, where I kept my eyes fixed on the boots of the person ahead. When fog rolled in, it was easy to see how a hiker might become disoriented and wander off the trail. Our guide, Farida, had an unflagging energy that amazed me. She walked to the front, then back to the end, checking on every straggler, including me, more than once. I reached the hut last, exhausted, but I have rarely felt prouder.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “tenderfoot” mean?
options: a gentle, kind person
a person whose feet are sore
the leader of a hiking group
someone who is afraid of heights
a beginner with little experience of rough outdoor life
the fastest walker in a group
qs.why: The narrator had just bought boots and was the least experienced hiker. The narrator's legs ached, but the word means a beginner, not someone with sore feet.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unflagging” mean?
options: nervous and unsure
careless and rushed
loud and cheerful
staying strong and steady without getting tired
quickly worn out
slowly fading as the day goes on
qs.why: Farida kept walking up and down the line all day, which amazed the tired narrator. Her energy did not fade.

qs.q: How does the narrator feel at the end of the hike?
options: Proud of being the first to reach the hut
Relieved that the hike was so easy
Proud of finishing, even though they were the least experienced and arrived last
Upset at having been lost in the fog
Angry at the guide for walking too fast
Embarrassed and determined never to hike again
qs.why: The narrator arrives last and exhausted but has “rarely felt prouder.” They were last, not first.

why: 'why' claimed sore feet 'may be true'; the passage mentions aching legs, not feet. Corrected the explanation.

set.text: In a village of four hundred people, scuttlebutt travels faster than the mail. So when a rumor spread that Hamid Karimi, the popular head of the volunteer fire service, had kept money from the summer fundraiser, half the village believed it by lunchtime. The source turned out to be Clive Dunmore, a well-known meddler who had once tried to run the fire service himself. For weeks he would badmouth Hamid to anyone who would listen. But the fundraiser's accounts had been checked by two independent volunteers, and every cent was in the bank. The story was pure calumny. The village council published the figures on the noticeboard, and Clive's attempt to besmirch his rival backfired. Hamid's reputation emerged untarnished, and at the next vote he won more support than any leader in the service's history.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “calumny” mean?
options: a public apology
a false statement made on purpose to damage someone's reputation
a friendly joke
an honest mistake
a careful check of the money
a true but embarrassing fact
qs.why: Clive spread a false story in an attempt to damage his rival's good name. Because it was meant to hurt Hamid, “an honest mistake” is wrong.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “besmirch” mean?
options: to damage someone's good name, often unfairly
to replace someone in a job
to attack someone physically
to cover something with mud
to demand an apology from someone
to praise someone in public
qs.why: Clive tried to ruin Hamid's reputation with a false rumor. The word can mean to make dirty, but here it is about a good name.

qs.q: Why did Hamid's reputation survive the rumor?
options: Nobody in the village believed the rumor
Independent checks showed all the money was in the bank, and the figures were made public
Hamid took Clive to court
Hamid paid the missing money back
Clive publicly apologized
The council removed Clive from the village
qs.why: The volunteers' check and the council's published figures proved the story false. In fact, half the village believed the rumor at first.

why: 'why' said Clive 'knew' the story was false, which the passage never states; reworded to what the text supports (a false story spread in an attempt to besmirch).

set.text: My father calls himself a proud troglodyte. He still writes paper checks, keeps phone numbers in a notebook, and owns a television so antediluvian that it has a dial. When my sister gave him a smart speaker for his birthday, he unplugged it within a week. “I don't need a machine listening to me,” he said. But there is a practical side to his resistance. He runs a printing shop, and he has watched expensive gadgetry come and go every few years, each new machine making the last one obsolescent before it had paid for itself. In the corner sits a superannuated fax machine that nobody has used in years. But his most reliable press, built in 1978, still handles the shop's workaday jobs: menus, wedding invitations, posters for lost cats. “Fashion changes,” he says. “A good machine just keeps working.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “obsolescent” mean?
options: fully paid for
brand new and modern
easy to use
broken beyond repair
very expensive
becoming out of date and starting to go out of use
qs.why: Each new machine makes the last one old-fashioned before it has paid for itself. The older machine still works, so it is not broken.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “workaday” mean?
options: badly paid
done only on weekends
extremely difficult
ordinary and everyday
special and exciting
done only by machines
qs.why: Menus, invitations and lost-cat posters are the shop's normal, everyday jobs, not special ones.

qs.q: What is the father's practical reason for keeping old machines?
options: He is angry with his sister
He does not know how to use modern devices
He cannot afford to buy any new machines
He has seen new technology lose its value quickly, while a good old machine keeps working
Old machines are more fashionable
His customers demand old-fashioned printing
qs.why: He watched new gadgets become outdated before paying for themselves, while his 1978 press still works. Nothing says he cannot afford new machines.

why: 'why' said money is not his reason, but 'before it had paid for itself' is partly about money; reworded so the distractor is ruled out accurately (nothing says he cannot afford them).
